summary:
Iris is a web-based prototype designed to make NASA's SPHEREx data accessible and interactive. SPHEREx surveys the entire sky in 102 near-infrared bands, creating an unprecedented opportunity to explore how celestial objects appear across different wavelengths and change over time.
Iris transforms this complex dataset into an intuitive sky explorer. Users can navigate by celestial coordinates or object names, explore the infrared sky across all 102 channels, extract quick-look spectral profiles, and identify celestial sources through astronomical catalog overlays and curated objects.
By combining astronomical visualization, spectral exploration, and accessible scientific context, Iris lowers the technical barriers to exploring SPHEREx data. Our goal is to provide a foundation for education, citizen science, and future investigations of moving and variable objects in the sky.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Iris is an interactive web prototype that makes NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations easier to explore through four interconnected workspaces:

Sky: An all-sky explorer powered by the SPHEREx DR1 spectral cube and Aladin Lite. Users navigate by coordinates or object names, explore 102 near-infrared channels, create RGB composites, and overlay astronomical catalogs such as SIMBAD, Gaia DR3, and CatWISE2020. A curated catalog highlights interesting celestial objects.

Plate: A scientific image inspector for selected sky regions. Iris supports SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images, allowing users to examine image data, variance, quality flags, and spectral channels.

When IRSA's discovery services are unavailable, Iris can access a limited index of Level-2 products on Amazon S3 or generate regional images directly from the DR1 All-Sky Cube using partial FITS reads. These fallback images preserve spectral exploration but do not contain individual observation dates. Users can also upload compatible SPHEREx FITS files for direct inspection.

Spectral Lab: Users can compare quick-look spectral profiles from up to eight sky positions across 102 channels, explore linear or logarithmic scales, and inspect the underlying numerical data.

Records: With cookie consent, users can save and revisit their selected regions.

Guided tours and an optional AI assistant help users understand the interface and navigate astronomical data.

BENEFITS AND EXPECTED IMPACT

SPHEREx produces enormous amounts of scientific data that can be difficult to explore without specialized tools.

Iris brings spatial, spectral, and potentially temporal exploration into one accessible interface, without requiring installation, accounts, or programming knowledge.

Our goal is to support astronomy education, encourage curiosity, and provide a foundation for citizen-science investigations of moving and variable celestial objects.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Aladin Lite, interactive spectral visualizations, React Joyride, Vitest, and Testing Library.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, Astroquery, reproject, NumPy, Pillow, httpx, and tenacity. SQLAlchemy, Alembic, and PostgreSQL support persistent records. The OpenAI SDK powers the optional assistant.

Infrastructure: Docker Compose, Traefik, HTTPS, and local caching.

Astronomical data: NASA's SPHEREx DR1 All-Sky Cube and Level-2 spectral products, accessed through HiPS, IRSA TAP, and public Amazon S3 storage. Additional astronomical information comes from SIMBAD, NED, Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, and curated local data.

CREATIVITY AND INNOVATION

Iris connects different ways of exploring the same astronomical region: navigating the infrared sky, inspecting scientific image data, and examining its spectral characteristics.

Its most distinctive technical contribution is a resilient data-access strategy. When external discovery services became unavailable, we developed an alternative that locates SPHEREx cube tiles spatially and retrieves only the required FITS data ranges from S3, enabling regional spectral exploration without downloading entire files.

Combined with an intuitive interface, guided exploration, and support for user-provided FITS files, Iris makes complex astronomical datasets more approachable.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific transparency: Quick-look spectral profiles are distinguished from calibrated source measurements. Estimated values are visually differentiated from observations, and unavailable temporal information is never presented as measured data.

Reliability: Multiple data-access strategies, caching, bounded retries, and explicit error states help the application remain useful during external service outages. The S3 cube fallback provides a reduced but functional exploration mode.

Usability: Clear navigation, guided tours, contextual information, and visual feedback help users explore unfamiliar scientific concepts.

Privacy: No user accounts are required. Optional persistent records use browser-specific identifiers and consent-based cookies.

Performance: Progressive HiPS loading, regional catalog queries, partial FITS downloads, and cached processing reduce unnecessary data transfers and help preserve a responsive viewing experience.
